source.citation: Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249-255.
source.finding: Students who read a passage and then tested themselves recalled more of it two days and one week later than students who reread it, even though the rereaders did slightly better after five minutes.
source.caveat: The original study used university students and prose passages. The effect has since been repeated many times with other ages and materials, which is why it is rated strong.

scenes.narration: Rereading your notes feels like revision. Mostly, it isn't.
The page looks familiar. So you feel like you know it. Familiar is not the same as remembered.
In 2006, two psychologists had students either reread a passage, or test themselves on it.
Five minutes later, the rereaders were ahead. A week later, the self-testers remembered more.
Pulling a fact out of your head is what strengthens it.
Today, close your book. Write down everything you remember from your last lesson. Then check what you missed.
